title.en: Two poems on love: Abhisara: The Tryst and Sonnet 116

hook.en: Two very different poets, a Bengali and an Englishman, three centuries apart, both ask what real love is. One answers with a story, the other with an argument.

objectives.en: Summarise the story of Abhisara: The Tryst in your own words
Explain the argument and structure of Sonnet 116
Compare the two poems' ideas of love

narration.en: Two very different poets, a Bengali and an Englishman, three centuries apart, both ask what real love is. One answers with a story, the other with an argument.

body.en: Based on a Buddhist legend, Tagore's poem tells of the young monk Upagupta, asleep by the city wall of Mathura, who is woken by Vasavadatta, a beautiful dancer, and invited to her home. He gently replies that the time has not yet come and he will visit her when it does. Months later, the same woman, struck by a deadly pestilence and cast out of the city, lies alone and suffering; Upagupta comes, tends her sores and comforts her, saying his time to visit has now come. The tryst is fulfilled not as passion but as compassion. Read the prescribed text itself; this guide is in our own words and quotes nothing.

points.en: Upagupta, a Buddhist monk; Vasavadatta, a dancer
First meeting: an invitation politely put off
Second meeting: she is sick and abandoned
True love as compassion, not desire

title.en: On the board: Sonnet 116: the argument

say.en: The speaker defines true love by saying what it is not, and then what it is.

text.en: Quatrain 1: love does not change when circumstances
change, or the loved one changes.
Quatrain 2: love is a fixed guide, like a sea-mark or
the star that sailors steer by, whatever the storm.
Quatrain 3: love is not ruled by Time; beauty fades,
but love lasts to the very end.
Couplet: if this is wrong, no one has ever loved
and the poet never wrote: a confident challenge.

text.en: Q2: love as a fixed guide

body.en: Sonnet 116 is a Shakespearean (English) sonnet: three quatrains and a rhyming couplet, rhymed ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, in iambic pentameter. The speaker defines ideal love as constant and unchanging. It does not bend when the beloved changes, it is a fixed mark that guides lost ships like the pole star, and it is not the plaything of Time, even though Time's sickle cuts down youthful beauty. The final couplet stakes the poet's whole reputation on the claim. Images come from the sea and from time: navigation, storms, the sickle.

points.en: Shakespearean sonnet: ABAB CDCD EFEF GG
Love is constant, a guiding star
Love outlasts Time; the couplet is a challenge

text.en: Love is shown through an act of care for the sick
Love is compared to a star that guides ships
Ends with a confident rhyming couplet
True love is more than physical beauty or desire
Told as a story with two meetings

explanation.en: Tagore tells a story of compassion; Shakespeare argues through images; both separate true love from attraction to beauty.

problem.en: Compare the idea of love in the two poems (in points).

steps.en: Both separate true love from physical attraction and passing beauty.
In Abhisara, love is shown through action: Upagupta's compassion when everyone else has abandoned Vasavadatta.
In Sonnet 116, love is defined in argument as a constant, unchanging bond.
Tagore's love is spiritual and universal; Shakespeare's is the ideal union of two minds.

answer.en: Both see true love as lasting beyond beauty; Tagore shows it as compassion, Shakespeare defines it as constancy.
